claim: Heparan sulfate (HS) is a glycosaminoglycan (GAG) comprised of repeating units of N-acetylglucosamine and glucuronic acid.
source: Degradation of heparan sulfate (HS), a glycosaminoglycan (GAG) comprised of repeating units of N-acetylglucosamine and glucuronic acid, begins in the cytosol and is completed in the lysosomes.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about the chemical composition of heparan sulfate, presented as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Degradation of heparan sulfate begins in the cytosol and is completed in the lysosomes.
source: Degradation of heparan sulfate (HS), a glycosaminoglycan (GAG) comprised of repeating units of N-acetylglucosamine and glucuronic acid, begins in the cytosol and is completed in the lysosomes.
evidence: This statement describes the cellular locations where HS degradation occurs, presented as established knowledge.

claim: Acetylation of the terminal non-reducing amino group of α-D-glucosamine of HS is essential for its complete breakdown into monosaccharides and free sulfate.
source: Acetylation of the terminal non-reducing amino group of α-D-glucosamine of HS is essential for its complete breakdown into monosaccharides and free sulfate.
evidence: This statement describes the necessity of acetylation for HS degradation, presented as established knowledge.

claim: HGSNAT is a resident of the lysosomal membrane.
source: Heparan-α-glucosaminide N-acetyltransferase (HGSNAT), a resident of the lysosomal membrane, catalyzes this essential acetylation reaction by accepting and transferring the acetyl group from cytosolic acetyl-CoA to terminal α-D-glucosamine of HS in the lysosomal lumen.
evidence: This describes the cellular localization of HGSNAT, presented as established knowledge.

claim: HGSNAT catalyzes the acetylation reaction by accepting and transferring the acetyl group from cytosolic acetyl-CoA to terminal α-D-glucosamine of HS in the lysosomal lumen.
source: Heparan-α-glucosaminide N-acetyltransferase (HGSNAT), a resident of the lysosomal membrane, catalyzes this essential acetylation reaction by accepting and transferring the acetyl group from cytosolic acetyl-CoA to terminal α-D-glucosamine of HS in the lysosomal lumen.
evidence: This describes the enzymatic function of HGSNAT, presented as established knowledge.

claim: Mutation-induced dysfunction in HGSNAT causes abnormal accumulation of HS within the lysosomes.
source: Mutation-induced dysfunction in HGSNAT causes abnormal accumulation of HS within the lysosomes and leads to an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disorder called mucopolysaccharidosis IIIC (MPS IIIC).
evidence: This describes the pathological consequence of HGSNAT dysfunction, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Mutation-induced dysfunction in HGSNAT leads to mucopolysaccharidosis IIIC (MPS IIIC), an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disorder.
source: Mutation-induced dysfunction in HGSNAT causes abnormal accumulation of HS within the lysosomes and leads to an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disorder called mucopolysaccharidosis IIIC (MPS IIIC).
evidence: This describes the disease caused by HGSNAT dysfunction, presented as established knowledge.

claim: There are no approved drugs or treatment strategies to cure or manage the symptoms of MPS IIIC.
source: There are no approved drugs or treatment strategies to cure or manage the symptoms of, MPS IIIC.
evidence: This statement about the lack of treatments is presented as current knowledge and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The authors determined a high-resolution structure of the HGSNAT-acetyl-CoA complex using cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM).
source: Here, we use cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to determine a high-resolution structure of the HGSNAT-acetyl-CoA complex, the first step in the HGSNAT-catalyzed acetyltransferase reaction.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The HGSNAT-acetyl-CoA complex structure represents the first step in the HGSNAT-catalyzed acetyltransferase reaction.
source: Here, we use cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to determine a high-resolution structure of the HGSNAT-acetyl-CoA complex, the first step in the HGSNAT-catalyzed acetyltransferase reaction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data, based on the presence of acetyl-CoA in the structure.

claim: The authors mapped known MPS IIIC mutations onto the HGSNAT structure.
source: In addition, we map the known MPS IIIC mutations onto the structure and elucidate the molecular basis for mutation-induced HGSNAT dysfunction.
evidence: This describes an analysis performed using the structure and known mutation data.

claim: The authors elucidated the molecular basis for mutation-induced HGSNAT dysfunction.
source: In addition, we map the known MPS IIIC mutations onto the structure and elucidate the molecular basis for mutation-induced HGSNAT dysfunction.
evidence: This describes an interpretation based on structural analysis of mutation sites.

claim: Dysfunction of enzymes in the GAG degradation pathway causes abnormal accumulation of partial degradation products within the lysosomes, resulting in mucopolysaccharidoses (MPSs).
source: Dysfunction, often inherited, of the enzymes involved in GAG degradation causes abnormal accumulation of the partial degradation products within the lysosomes, resulting in mucopolysaccharidoses (MPSs), a collective term for the group of rare autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorders characterized by the accumulation of partially degraded GAGs (Coutinho et al., 2012; Huizing and Gahl, 2020; Klein et al., 1978; Platt et al., 2018; Ruivo et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Mucopolysaccharidoses (MPSs) are rare autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorders characterized by the accumulation of partially degraded GAGs.
source: Dysfunction, often inherited, of the enzymes involved in GAG degradation causes abnormal accumulation of the partial degradation products within the lysosomes, resulting in mucopolysaccharidoses (MPSs), a collective term for the group of rare autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorders characterized by the accumulation of partially degraded GAGs (Coutinho et al., 2012; Huizing and Gahl, 2020; Klein et al., 1978; Platt et al., 2018; Ruivo et al., 2009).
evidence: This definitional statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Impairment of enzymes in the HS degradation pathway causes mucopolysaccharidosis III (MPS III), or Sanfilippo's syndrome.
source: HS is a GAG made of repeating units of N-acetylglucosamine and glucuronic acid, and impairment of enzymes in the HS degradation pathway causes mucopolysaccharidosis III (MPS III), or Sanfilippo's syndrome that is characterized by abnormal storage of HS degradation pathway intermediates within the lysosomes in all organs and excretion of these intermediates in the urine.
evidence: This statement describes the disease caused by HS degradation pathway dysfunction, presented as established knowledge.

claim: MPS III is characterized by abnormal storage of HS degradation pathway intermediates within the lysosomes in all organs and excretion of these intermediates in the urine.
source: HS is a GAG made of repeating units of N-acetylglucosamine and glucuronic acid, and impairment of enzymes in the HS degradation pathway causes mucopolysaccharidosis III (MPS III), or Sanfilippo's syndrome that is characterized by abnormal storage of HS degradation pathway intermediates within the lysosomes in all organs and excretion of these intermediates in the urine.
evidence: This describes the pathological features of MPS III, presented as established knowledge.

claim: Symptoms of MPS III include organomegaly, abnormal joint mobility, compromised cardiac function, degeneration of vision and hearing, and dementia.
source: The onset of the symptoms of MPS III, which include organomegaly, abnormal joint mobility, compromised cardiac function, degeneration of vision and hearing, and dementia, often begins in juveniles and ends in premature death.
evidence: This lists clinical manifestations of MPS III, presented as established knowledge.

claim: The onset of MPS III symptoms often begins in juveniles and ends in premature death.
source: The onset of the symptoms of MPS III, which include organomegaly, abnormal joint mobility, compromised cardiac function, degeneration of vision and hearing, and dementia, often begins in juveniles and ends in premature death.
evidence: This describes the typical disease course, presented as established knowledge.

claim: Currently, no therapies for MPS III are available.
source: Currently, no therapies for MPS III are available (Coutinho et al., 2012; Huizing and Gahl, 2020; McBride and Flanigan, 2021; Pshezhetsky et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement about the lack of available therapies is supported by citations.

claim: MPS III is classified into four subtypes – MPS IIIA-IIID, depending on the dysfunctional enzyme.
source: Depending on the dysfunctional enzyme, MPS III is classified into four subtypes – MPS IIIA-IIID.
evidence: This describes the classification system for MPS III, presented as established knowledge.

claim: MPS IIIC has a prevalence rate of 1 in 1.4 million.
source: Of these four MPS III subtypes, MPS IIIC (prevalence rate of 1 in 1.4 million) is caused by the dysfunction of heparan-α-glucosaminide N-acetyltransferase (HGSNAT, EC 2.3.1.78).
evidence: This provides epidemiological data about MPS IIIC prevalence.

claim: MPS IIIC is caused by the dysfunction of HGSNAT.
source: Of these four MPS III subtypes, MPS IIIC (prevalence rate of 1 in 1.4 million) is caused by the dysfunction of heparan-α-glucosaminide N-acetyltransferase (HGSNAT, EC 2.3.1.78).
evidence: This describes the molecular cause of MPS IIIC, supported by citations.

claim: HGSNAT is the only enzyme of the GAG pathway that is not a hydrolase.
source: HGSNAT is the only enzyme of the GAG pathway that is not a hydrolase.
evidence: This distinguishes HGSNAT from other GAG pathway enzymes, presented as established knowledge.

claim: HGSNAT catalyzes the only known biosynthetic reaction of the GAG degradation pathway within the lysosome.
source: It catalyzes the only known biosynthetic reaction of the GAG degradation pathway within the lysosome, that is, the acetyl-CoA (ACO) mediated N-acetylation of the terminal non-reducing amino group of α-D-glucosamine (Fan et al., 2006; Hrebícek et al., 2006; Huizing and Gahl, 2020; Klein et al., 1978; Nagel et al., 2019; Pshezhetsky et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the unique enzymatic function of HGSNAT, supported by citations.

claim: Acetylation of the terminal α-D-glucosamine group is essential for subsequent HS degradation within the lysosomes.
source: Acetylation of the terminal α-D-glucosamine group is essential for subsequent HS degradation within the lysosomes.
evidence: This describes the functional importance of HGSNAT's enzymatic activity, presented as established knowledge.

claim: HGSNAT is not homologous to any known proteins, including acetyl-CoA binding proteins, N-acetyltransferases, and other lysosomal proteins.
source: HGSNAT is not homologous to any known proteins, including acetyl-CoA binding proteins, N-acetyltransferases, and other lysosomal proteins.
evidence: This describes the lack of sequence homology, which can be inferred from sequence database searches.

claim: HGSNAT mRNA has two translation start sites (M1 and M29), yielding two functionally active isoforms (73 kDa and 70 kDa) of HGSNAT.
source: HGSNAT mRNA has two translation start sites (M1 and M29), yielding two functionally active isoforms (73 kDa and 70 kDa) of HGSNAT, both targeted to the lysosomal membrane (Durand et al., 2010; Fan et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the molecular biology of HGSNAT expression, supported by citations.

claim: Both isoforms of HGSNAT are targeted to the lysosomal membrane.
source: HGSNAT mRNA has two translation start sites (M1 and M29), yielding two functionally active isoforms (73 kDa and 70 kDa) of HGSNAT, both targeted to the lysosomal membrane (Durand et al., 2010; Fan et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the cellular localization of both HGSNAT isoforms, supported by citations.

claim: The study uses isoform 2 of HGSNAT, which is produced as a 635 amino acid protein containing a 30 amino acid N-terminal signal peptide, a ~110 amino acid long luminal domain, and 11 transmembrane helices (TMs).
source: In this study, we use isoform 2 of HGSNAT, which is produced as a 635 amino acid protein containing a 30 amino acid N-terminal signal peptide, a ~110 amino acid long luminal domain, and 11 transmembrane helices (TMs).
evidence: This describes the specific isoform used in the study and its structural features.

claim: HGSNAT is believed to be expressed in the cell as an immature precursor protein that localizes as an N-glycosylated dimer on the lysosomal membrane.
source: HGSNAT is believed to be expressed in the cell as an immature precursor protein that localizes as an N-glycosylated dimer on the lysosomal membrane (Durand et al., 2010; Fan et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the biosynthesis and localization of HGSNAT, supported by citations.

claim: The localization of HGSNAT happens via the adaptor protein-mediated pathway, aided by the lysosomal targeting motifs [DE]-XXXL[LI] (204ETDRLI209) and YXXØ (624YILYRKK630) present towards the N- and C-terminus of HGSNAT, respectively.
source: The localization of HGSNAT happens via the adaptor protein-mediated pathway, aided by the lysosomal targeting motifs [DE]-XXXL[LI] (204ETDRLI209) and YXXØ (624YILYRKK630) present towards the N- and C-terminus of HGSNAT, respectively (Rudnik and Damme, 2021; Schwake et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of HGSNAT trafficking, supported by citations.

claim: Deleting the C-terminal lysosomal sorting signal in HGSNAT retains the protein in the plasma membrane.
source: Deleting the C-terminal lysosomal sorting signal in HGSNAT retains the protein in the plasma membrane (Bonifacino and Traub, 2003; Durand et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes the effect of deleting the sorting signal, supported by citations.

claim: Once targeted to the lysosomal membrane, HGSNAT is proteolyzed by unidentified acid proteases in the lysosomal lumen into two unequal fragments - a smaller luminal N-terminal α-HGSNAT and a larger transmembrane C-terminal β-HGSNAT that continue to co-localize despite the proteolysis.
source: Once targeted to the lysosomal membrane, HGSNAT, like a few other lysosomal membrane proteins, is proteolyzed by unidentified acid proteases in the lysosomal lumen into two unequal fragments - a smaller luminal N-terminal α-HGSNAT and a larger transmembrane C-terminal β-HGSNAT that continue to co-localize despite the proteolysis (Durand et al., 2010; Fan et al., 2011; Rudnik and Damme, 2021; Steenhuis et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the proteolytic processing of HGSNAT, supported by citations.

claim: Upon proteolytic maturation, it is believed that HGSNAT is assembled as a hetero oligomer of α- & β-HGSNAT chains.
source: Upon proteolytic maturation, it is believed that HGSNAT is assembled as a hetero oligomer of α- & β-HGSNAT chains (Durand et al., 2010; Feldhammer et al., 2009b).
evidence: This describes the proposed oligomeric state of mature HGSNAT, supported by citations.

claim: The essentiality of proteolytic cleavage and oligomerization for HGSNAT activity remains debated.
source: However, the essentiality of proteolytic cleavage and oligomerization for HGSNAT activity remains debated as endoplasmic reticulum (ER) retained monomeric HGSNAT was also shown to be active (Durand et al., 2010; Fan et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes an ongoing debate in the field, supported by citations showing conflicting evidence.

claim: Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) retained monomeric HGSNAT was shown to be active.
source: However, the essentiality of proteolytic cleavage and oligomerization for HGSNAT activity remains debated as endoplasmic reticulum (ER) retained monomeric HGSNAT was also shown to be active (Durand et al., 2010; Fan et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes experimental findings from prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: Over 70 unique mutations in the HGSNAT (TMEM76) gene have been identified.
source: So far, over 70 unique mutations in the HGSNAT (TMEM76) gene have been identified.
evidence: This provides a count of known mutations, which can be verified from mutation databases and citations.

claim: HGSNAT mutations include deletions, nonsense mutations, splice-site variants, and silent and missense mutations.
source: These mutations span the entire sequence and include deletions, nonsense mutations, splice-site variants, and silent and missense mutations (Canals et al., 2011; Fan et al., 2006; Fedele and Hopwood, 2010; Feldhammer et al., 2009a; Feldhammer et al., 2009b; Hrebícek et al., 2006; Huizing and Gahl, 2020).
evidence: This categorizes the types of mutations found in HGSNAT, supported by citations.

claim: The majority of the mutations that cause MPS IIIC are missense mutations that result in HGSNAT folding and localization defects.
source: The majority of the mutations that cause MPS IIIC are missense mutations that result in HGSNAT folding and localization defects, making them ideal targets for pharmacochaperone therapy.
evidence: This describes the predominant type of pathogenic mutations and their effects, supported by citations.

claim: Missense mutations that cause MPS IIIC are ideal targets for pharmacochaperone therapy.
source: The majority of the mutations that cause MPS IIIC are missense mutations that result in HGSNAT folding and localization defects, making them ideal targets for pharmacochaperone therapy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of the mutations and the mechanism of pharmacochaperone therapy.

claim: Site-specific inhibitors of HGSNAT activity have been explored as agents to rescue the misfolded conformation of certain missense variants, thereby restoring the partial N-acetyltransferase activity.
source: Site-specific inhibitors of HGSNAT activity have been explored as agents to rescue the misfolded conformation of certain missense variants, thereby restoring the partial N-acetyltransferase activity (Coutinho et al., 2012; Fedele and Hopwood, 2010; Feldhammer et al., 2009b; Pan et al., 2022).
evidence: This describes therapeutic approaches that have been investigated, supported by citations.

claim: This is the first structure of a member of the transmembrane acyl transferase (TmAT) superfamily.
source: This is the first structure of a member of the transmembrane acyl transferase (TmAT) superfamily (classes 9.B.97 and 9.B.169 in the Transporter Classification Database (TCDB)) (Saier et al., 2021).
evidence: This claims novelty for the structure, which can be verified by checking structural databases.

claim: The HGSNAT-acetyl-CoA complex structure provides a high-resolution snapshot of the first step in HGSNAT catalyzed acetyltransferase reaction.
source: The HGSNAT-acetyl-CoA complex structure presented here provides a high-resolution snapshot of the first step in HGSNAT catalyzed acetyltransferase reaction, and reveals critical cofactor binding amino acids in the HGSNAT active site.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The HGSNAT structure reveals critical cofactor binding amino acids in the HGSNAT active site.
source: The HGSNAT-acetyl-CoA complex structure presented here provides a high-resolution snapshot of the first step in HGSNAT catalyzed acetyltransferase reaction, and reveals critical cofactor binding amino acids in the HGSNAT active site.
evidence: This describes findings from the structural analysis.

claim: The structure provides molecular insights into the impact of MPS IIIC-causing mutations on acetyl-CoA binding and the overall architecture of the protein.
source: In addition, our structure also provides molecular insights into the impact of MPS IIIC-causing mutations on acetyl-CoA binding and the overall architecture of the protein.
evidence: This describes insights gained from mapping mutations onto the structure.

claim: Two groups have previously reported purification of HGSNAT in varying oligomeric forms.
source: Two groups have previously reported purification of HGSNAT in varying oligomeric forms (Durand et al., 2010; Fan et al., 2011; Feldhammer et al., 2009b).
evidence: This summarizes prior work, supported by citations.

claim: The first group used non-ionic surfactants, NP-40 and Triton X-100, in their purification experiments and observed dimers and hexamers of HGSNAT.
source: The first group used non-ionic surfactants, NP-40 and Triton X-100, in their purification experiments and observed dimers and hexamers of HGSNAT.
evidence: This describes methods and results from prior work, supported by citations.

claim: The PEG-based headgroup in NP-40 and Triton X-100 is relatively bulky and yields micelles of variable sizes (45–100 kDa) and has been known to cause sample heterogeneity in eukaryotic membrane proteins.
source: The PEG-based headgroup in these detergents is relatively bulky and yields micelles of variable sizes (45–100 kDa) and has been known to cause sample heterogeneity in eukaryotic membrane proteins (Orwick-Rydmark et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes properties of detergents, supported by a citation.

claim: The second group purified monomeric HGSNAT using non-ionic detergent DDM, which forms a relatively uniform, albeit large, micelle (98 kDa).
source: The second group purified monomeric HGSNAT using non-ionic detergent DDM, which forms a relatively uniform, albeit large, micelle (98 kDa).
evidence: This describes methods and results from prior work, with information about DDM properties.

claim: The authors transfected HEK293 GnTI- cells with plasmids expressing either N-terminal or C-terminal GFP-fusion of HGSNAT and monitored GFP fluorescence in detergent-solubilized HGSNAT lysates by fluorescence-detection size-exclusion chromatography (FSEC).
source: To identify the ideal conditions for expression and purification of monodisperse HGSNAT, we transfected HEK293 GnTI- cells with plasmids expressing either N-terminal or C-terminal GFP-fusion of HGSNAT and monitored GFP fluorescence in detergent-solubilized HGSNAT lysates by fluorescence-detection size-exclusion chromatography (FSEC) (Kawate and Gouaux, 2006).
evidence: This describes experimental methods used in the study.

claim: The position of GFP did not alter the expression of HGSNAT.
source: We noticed that the position of GFP did not alter the expression of HGSNAT (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: The HGSNAT dimer model predicted using ColabFold suggested that the C-termini of the protomers lie at the dimer interface.
source: However, the HGSNAT dimer model predicted using ColabFold suggested that the C-termini of the protomers lie at the dimer interface (Mirdita et al., 2022).
evidence: This describes a computational prediction, supported by a citation to the prediction method.

claim: For large-scale production of HGSNAT for structural studies, the authors expressed N-terminal StrepII-tag-GFP-HGSNAT fusion.
source: Thus, for large-scale production of HGSNAT for structural studies, we expressed N-terminal StrepII-tag-GFP-HGSNAT fusion.
evidence: This describes the expression construct used in the study.

claim: Large quantities of GFP-HGSNAT fusion were produced using baculovirus-mediated transduction of HEK293 GnTI- cells.
source: Large quantities of GFP-HGSNAT fusion were produced using baculovirus-mediated transduction of HEK293 GnTI- cells (Goehring et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the expression method used, with a citation to the method.

claim: Reducing the temperature of the suspension cell culture to 32 °C at about 8–10 hr after transduction resulted in a better yield than continuing to grow cells at 37 °C.
source: We found that reducing the temperature of the suspension cell culture to 32 °C at about 8–10 hr after transduction, or transient transfection, resulted in a better yield than continuing to grow cells at 37 °C (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This describes an experimental optimization, supported by data in a figure.

claim: In most of the detergent conditions tested, HGSNAT was predominantly dimeric.
source: In most of the detergent conditions we tested, HGSNAT was predominantly dimeric (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–H).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in figures.

claim: HGSNAT appeared most stable in digitonin based on single-point thermal melt tests.
source: HGSNAT appeared most stable in digitonin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I–L).
evidence: This is a conclusion from experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The authors purified HGSNAT in digitonin based on FSEC analysis of relative thermal stability and homogeneity.
source: Based on our FSEC analysis of relative thermal stability and homogeneity, we purified HGSNAT in digitonin.
evidence: This describes the rationale for choosing digitonin, based on experimental data.

claim: The authors observed a dimer in chromatography experiments and a band corresponding to a monomer on SDS-PAGE.
source: We observed a dimer in our chromatography experiments and a band corresponding to a monomer on SDS-PAGE (Figure 1—figure supplement 1M–O).
evidence: This describes experimental observations shown in figures.

claim: The authors solved the structure of HGSNAT in complex with acetyl-CoA (HGSNAT-ACO complex) to a global resolution of 3.26 Å.
source: We solved the structure of HGSNAT in complex with acetyl-CoA (HGSNAT-ACO complex) to a global resolution of 3.26 Å, with the transmembrane domain (TMD) being better resolved than the luminal domain (LD) (Table 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by structural data.

claim: The transmembrane domain (TMD) is better resolved than the luminal domain (LD) in the HGSNAT structure.
source: We solved the structure of HGSNAT in complex with acetyl-CoA (HGSNAT-ACO complex) to a global resolution of 3.26 Å, with the transmembrane domain (TMD) being better resolved than the luminal domain (LD) (Table 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This describes the quality of different regions in the structure.

claim: This is the first experimentally determined structure of a member of the TmAT protein family.
source: This is the first experimentally determined structure of a member of the protein family (TmAT).
evidence: This claims novelty, which can be verified by checking structural databases.

claim: HGSNAT is a dimer where the protomers are related to each other by twofold rotational symmetry, and the C2 axis of rotation is perpendicular to the plane of the membrane.
source: Our structure reveals that HGSNAT is a dimer where the protomers are related to each other by twofold rotational symmetry, and the C2 axis of rotation is perpendicular to the plane of the membrane (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This describes the overall architecture observed in the structure.

claim: Each polypeptide of HGSNAT has an N-terminal LD followed by 11 TMs that comprise the TMD, which is ensconced in the lysosomal membrane.
source: Each polypeptide of HGSNAT has an N-terminal LD followed by 11 TMs that comprise the TMD, which is ensconced in the lysosomal membrane.
evidence: This describes the domain organization observed in the structure.

claim: The authors could model all the secondary structure elements of the protein unambiguously except the first 48 amino acids including the N-terminal signal peptide and the cytoplasmic loop 1 (CL1; L183-L236).
source: We could model all the secondary structure elements of the protein unambiguously except the first 48 amino acids including the N-terminal signal peptide and the cytoplasmic loop 1 (CL1; L183-L236).
evidence: This describes the completeness of the structural model.

claim: The regions that are poorly resolved are the β-turn that connects β7 and β8 (N140-E148) and the C-terminal half of TM1 (V176-F181).
source: The regions that are poorly resolved are the β-turn that connects β7 and β8 (N140-E148) the C-terminal half of TM1 (V176-F181) (Figure 1A, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3D and E).
