claim: The C-terminus of the protein lies at the dimer interface but is unlikely to be directly involved in dimerization as the C-termini of the protomers lie ~25 Å away from each other.
source: The C-terminus of the protein lies at the dimer interface but is unlikely to be directly involved in dimerization as the C-termini of the protomers lie ~25 Å away from each other, pointing towards the central acetyl-CoA binding site (ACOS) (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data showing the distance between C-termini.

claim: The TMD of the HGSNAT protomer comprises a central 4+4 fold, where TMs 2–5 are related to TMs 6–9 by a twofold rotational pseudo-symmetry with the axis of rotation being perpendicular to the plane of the membrane.
source: The TMD of the HGSNAT protomer comprises of a central 4+4 fold, where the TMs 2–5 are related to TMs 6–9 by a twofold rotational pseudo-symmetry with the axis of rotation being perpendicular to the plane of the membrane (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This describes the internal symmetry observed in the TMD structure.

claim: TMs 2–5, along with TM10, form a 'catalytic core' and enclose the ACOS accessible via the cytosol and lumen along the dimer interface.
source: TMs 2–5, along with TM10, form a 'catalytic core' and enclose the ACOS accessible via the cytosol and lumen along the dimer interface.
evidence: This describes the functional organization of the TMD based on the structure.

claim: ACOSs of the protomers lie on either side of the dimer interface axis.
source: ACOSs of the protomers lie on either side of the dimer interface axis.
evidence: This describes the spatial arrangement of active sites in the dimer.

claim: TMs 6–9, along with TM11, form a 'scaffold domain' separated from the dimer interface by the catalytic core.
source: TMs 6–9, along with TM11, form a 'scaffold domain' separated from the dimer interface by the catalytic core (Figure 1E).
evidence: This describes the functional organization of the TMD based on the structure.

claim: The third luminal loop (LL3) connecting TM6 and TM7 forms a lid that limits the access to the cavity between the catalytic core and the scaffold domain from the luminal side.
source: The third luminal loop (LL3) connecting TM6 and TM7 forms a lid that limits the access to the cavity between the catalytic core and the scaffold domain from the luminal side (Figure 1A, C and D).
evidence: This describes a structural feature and its functional implication.

claim: The TMD region comprising TM2-TM11 of HGSNAT is predicted to be evolutionarily conserved across HGSNATs from other kingdoms.
source: The TMD region comprising TM2-TM11 of HGSNAT is predicted to be evolutionarily conserved across HGSNATs from other kingdoms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on sequence conservation analysis shown in a figure.

claim: The authors named the unique architecture of HGSNAT the transmembrane N-acetyltransferase (TNAT) fold.
source: Owing to the unique architecture we have named this novel fold as the transmembrane N-acetyltransferase (TNAT) fold.
evidence: This is a naming decision based on the novelty of the fold.

claim: The ACOS in the HGSNAT structure is relatively more accessible from the luminal side than the cytosolic side, as the nucleoside head group of the bound acetyl-CoA blocks the cytosolic entrance of ACOS.
source: The ACOS in our structure is relatively more accessible from the luminal side than the cytosolic side, as the nucleoside head group of the bound acetyl-CoA blocks the cytosolic entrance of ACOS (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure about the accessibility of the active site.

claim: The HGSNAT-ACO complex is in a conformation where the active site is readily accessible for the binding of the second substrate from the lysosomal lumen.
source: Thus, the HGSNAT-ACO complex is in a conformation where the active site is readily accessible for the binding of the second substrate from the lysosomal lumen.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed accessibility of the active site.

claim: The LDs of the protomers lie diagonally opposite to each other ~45 Å away from the dimer interface and are not involved in dimerization.
source: The LDs of the protomers lie diagonally opposite to each other ~45 Å away from the dimer interface and are not involved in dimerization (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the spatial arrangement of the LDs and their lack of involvement in dimerization.

claim: LD is a ~110 amino acids long β-sandwich made of two beta sheets of four strands each.
source: Located between the N-terminal signal peptide and the TM1, LD is a~110 amino acids long β-sandwich made of two beta sheets of four strands each where strands β1, β4, β7, & β8 form the mixed β-sheet on top (Figure 1A–E, blue), and the strands β2, β3, β5, & β6 arrange as bottom anti-parallel β-sheet (Figure 1A–E, gray).
evidence: This describes the secondary structure of the LD observed in the structure.

claim: Strands β1, β4, β7, & β8 form the mixed β-sheet on top of the LD.
source: Located between the N-terminal signal peptide and the TM1, LD is a~110 amino acids long β-sandwich made of two beta sheets of four strands each where strands β1, β4, β7, & β8 form the mixed β-sheet on top (Figure 1A–E, blue), and the strands β2, β3, β5, & β6 arrange as bottom anti-parallel β-sheet (Figure 1A–E, gray).
evidence: This describes the strand arrangement in the LD structure.

claim: Strands β2, β3, β5, & β6 arrange as bottom anti-parallel β-sheet of the LD.
source: Located between the N-terminal signal peptide and the TM1, LD is a~110 amino acids long β-sandwich made of two beta sheets of four strands each where strands β1, β4, β7, & β8 form the mixed β-sheet on top (Figure 1A–E, blue), and the strands β2, β3, β5, & β6 arrange as bottom anti-parallel β-sheet (Figure 1A–E, gray).
evidence: This describes the strand arrangement in the LD structure.

claim: The mixed β-sheet is arranged such that the order of the strands is β4-β1-β7-β8, with β1 & β7 being parallel.
source: The mixed β-sheet is arranged such that the order of the strands is β4-β1-β7-β8, with β1 & β7 being parallel.
evidence: This describes the detailed arrangement of strands in the mixed β-sheet.

claim: β8 of LD is connected to TM1.
source: β8 of LD is connected to TM1 (Figures 1B, D, 2A).
evidence: This describes the connectivity between LD and TMD.

claim: LD has two predicted disulfide bonds – one in the β-turn that connects β2 and β3 (C76-C79), and the other between the strands β6 and β8 (C123-C151).
source: LD has two predicted disulfide bonds – one in the β-turn that connects β2 and β3 (C76-C79), and the other between the strands β6 and β8 (C123-C151) holding the two sheets together.
evidence: This describes predicted disulfide bonds based on cysteine positions.

claim: The resolution of the LD domain allows unambiguous modeling of only one disulfide bond (C76-C79).
source: The resolution of the LD domain in our structure allows us to model only one (C76-C79) of these unambiguously (Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes a limitation of the structural data.

claim: HGSNAT is produced as a pro-protein that is believed to get proteolyzed into two fragments, HGSNAT-α and HGSNAT-β, of unequal sizes, which remain together.
source: HGSNAT is produced as a pro-protein that is believed to get proteolyzed into two fragments, HGSNAT-α and HGSNAT-β, of unequal sizes, which remain together (Durand et al., 2010; Fan et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the biosynthesis of HGSNAT, supported by citations.

claim: It is unclear if HGSNAT-α is made of just LD or LD and TM1, and if HGSNAT-β is made of all TMs or only TMs2-11.
source: It is unclear if HGSNAT-α is made of just LD or LD and TM1, and if HGSNAT-β is made of all TMs or only TMs2-11 (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes uncertainty about the exact boundaries of the proteolytic fragments.

claim: The FSEC and SDS-PAGE analyses of the purified protein indicate that the recombinant HGSNAT is not proteolyzed.
source: While our structure has relatively poor local resolution at the predicted protease sites, making it difficult to map them unambiguously, the FSEC nor the SDS-PAGE analyses of the purified protein indicate that the recombinant HGSNAT is not proteolyzed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data.

claim: The relatively low local resolution of LD is because of the flexibility introduced by GFP fused to the N-term of HGSNAT.
source: We believe the relatively low local resolution of LD is because of the flexibility introduced by GFP fused to the N-term of HGSNAT.
evidence: This is a speculation about the cause of poor resolution in the LD.

claim: LD interacts with TMD at multiple sites via an extensive interaction network that spans ~35 Å, comprised of a salt bridge (D52-H605), hydrogen bonds, and dipole-dipole and hydrophobic interactions.
source: LD interacts with TMD at multiple sites via an extensive interaction network that spans ~35 Å, comprised of a salt bridge (D52-H605), hydrogen bonds, and dipole-dipole and hydrophobic interactions (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This describes the LD-TMD interface observed in the structure.

claim: The N-terminus of TM11 interacts with the N-terminus of β1 and LL1.
source: The N-terminus of TM11 interacts with the N-terminus of β1 and LL1.
evidence: This describes specific interactions at the LD-TMD interface.

claim: LL1 also interacts with the N-terminus of TM1 and the β4-β5 turn.
source: LL1 also interacts with the N-terminus of TM1 and the β4-β5 turn.
evidence: This describes specific interactions at the LD-TMD interface.

claim: The β2-β3 turn, including the C76-C79 disulfide, interacts extensively with LL3 and is a part of LL4.
source: The β2-β3 turn, including the C76-C79 disulfide, interacts extensively with LL3 and is a part of LL4.
evidence: This describes specific interactions at the LD-TMD interface.

claim: The β2-β3 turn-LL3-LL4 interaction is stabilized by a 3π-network formed by the stacking of Y77, H78, & F428 side chains.
source: The β2-β3 turn-LL3-LL4 interaction is also stabilized by a 3π-network formed by the stacking of Y77, H78, & F428 side chains.
evidence: This describes a specific stabilizing interaction at the LD-TMD interface.

claim: The hydrogen bond network that stabilizes the LD-TMD interaction is formed between the amino acids M51, H78, and S162 of LD with H605 and Q603, D427 and F428, and Y264 of the TMD, respectively.
source: The hydrogen bond network that stabilizes the LD-TMD interaction is formed between the amino acids M51, H78, and S162 of LD with H605 and Q603, D427 and F428, and Y264 of the TMD, respectively (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This describes specific hydrogen bonds at the LD-TMD interface.

claim: The LD-TMD interface is separated from the dimer interface by the central catalytic core.
source: The LD-TMD interface is separated from the dimer interface by the central catalytic core (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This describes the spatial relationship between different interfaces.

claim: The dimer interface is spread across ~35 Å towards the luminal side of the protein, perpendicular to the C2 rotation axis.
source: The dimer interface is spread across ~35 Å towards the luminal side of the protein, perpendicular to the C2 rotation axis (Figure 2C).
evidence: This describes the extent and orientation of the dimer interface.

claim: Although TMs 4, 10, and 11 from both protomers lie on either side of the dimer interface, they do not directly interact to stabilize the dimer interface.
source: Although the TMs 4, 10, and 11 from both protomers lie on either side of the dimer interface, they do not directly interact to stabilize the dimer interface.
evidence: This is an observation about which TMs are not involved in dimerization.

claim: The primary mediator of dimerization is the disulfide between C334s within the LL2s of each protomer.
source: The primary mediator of dimerization is the disulfide between C334s within the LL2s of each protomer (Figure 2C, rectangle inset).
evidence: This describes the main interaction stabilizing the dimer.

claim: In addition to the C334-C334 disulfide, the dimer interface is also stabilized by an extensive π-π interaction network formed between the aromatic residues of LL2 (332-340) of one protomer and the aromatic residues of LL5 (588-598) of the other protomer.
source: In addition to the C334-C334 disulfide, the dimer interface is also stabilized by an extensiveπ-π interaction network formed between the aromatic residues of LL2 (332-340) of one protomer and the aromatic residues of LL5 (588-598) of the other protomer (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This describes additional interactions stabilizing the dimer interface.

claim: The aromatic bulky side chains at the dimer interface are buried in the membrane, and the hydrophilic residues face the lumen.
source: Notably, the aromatic bulky side chains at the interface are buried in the membrane, and the hydrophilic residues face the lumen (Figure 2C, oval inset).
evidence: This describes the orientation of residues at the dimer interface.

claim: Y333, L338, and S339 of LL2 from one protomer form a series of hydrogen bonds with F593 and K598 of LL5 of the other protomer.
source: Y333, L338, and S339 of LL2 from one protomer form a series of hydrogen bonds with F593 and K598 of LL5 of the other protomer, which adds to the stabilization of the dimer interface (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This describes specific hydrogen bonds at the dimer interface.

claim: In all the detergents tested, HGSNAT eluted as a dimer.
source: In all the detergents we tested, HGSNAT eluted as a dimer, a testimony to the extensive side-chain interaction network.
evidence: This is an experimental observation supporting the stability of the dimer.

claim: The twofold rotational symmetry between the protomers juxtaposes the ACOSs of protomers connecting them with each other on the cytosolic side.
source: The twofold rotational symmetry between the protomers juxtaposes the ACOSs of protomers connecting them with each other on the cytosolic side (Figures 1 and 2C).
evidence: This describes the spatial relationship between active sites in the dimer.

claim: The interconnected space between ACOSs is partitioned by lipids, preventing the diffusion of ligands from one active site to the other within a dimer.
source: This interconnected space is partitioned by lipids, preventing the diffusion of ligands from one active site to the other within a dimer (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure showing ordered lipid density.

claim: The authors generated two HGSNAT mutants of residues at the dimer interface – C334A and F593A.
source: We generated two HGSNAT mutants of residues at the dimer interface – C334A and F593A.
evidence: This describes experimental work to test the importance of dimer interface residues.

claim: In both C334A and F593A mutants, the overall expression of HGSNAT was not reduced.
source: In both these mutants, the overall expression of HGSNAT was not reduced.
evidence: This is an experimental observation about mutant expression levels.

claim: In the F593A mutant, the stability of the dimer remained unaffected.
source: In the case of F593A, the stability of the dimer also remained unaffected (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,H,I and N).
evidence: This is an experimental observation about the F593A mutant.

claim: Both C334A and F593A mutants still expressed predominantly as dimers even in the presence of 1% digitonin.
source: While both these mutants still expressed predominantly as dimers even in the presence of 1% digitonin, the C334A mutant eluted as a monomer upon heat treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,H,I and K).
evidence: This is an experimental observation about the oligomeric state of mutants.

claim: The C334A mutant eluted as a monomer upon heat treatment.
source: While both these mutants still expressed predominantly as dimers even in the presence of 1% digitonin, the C334A mutant eluted as a monomer upon heat treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,H,I and K).
evidence: This is an experimental observation showing the effect of breaking the disulfide bond.

claim: In the absence of the C334-C334 disulfide, the extensive side-chain interaction network stabilizes the dimer interface at room temperature, but heating destabilizes these interactions, resulting in a monomeric C334A.
source: As C334A breaks a covalent disulfide link between the protomers, in the absence of this disulfide, the extensive side-chain interaction network stabilizes the dimer interface. Heating destabilizes these interactions, resulting in a monomeric C334A.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results for the C334A mutant.

claim: MOLEonline predicted the presence of a ~75 Å pore within the TMD, that begins at the cytosolic side and extends to the luminal side.
source: We used MOLEonline to predict the presence of a~75 Å pore within the TMD, that begins at the cytosolic side and extends to the luminal side (Pravda et al., 2018; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes a computational prediction using the structure.

claim: The pore predicted by MOLEonline is lined by highly conserved residues of TMs 2–5 and TM 10.
source: The pore predicted by MOLEonline is lined by highly conserved residues of the TMs 2–5 and TM 10 (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This combines computational prediction with conservation analysis.

claim: The helix TM10 is bent by ~80° such that the luminal-side 2/3rd (TM10b) of the helix is parallel to TM2 and the cytosolic-side 1/3rd (TM10a) of the helix protrudes between TM2 and TM11.
source: We note that the helix TM10 is bent by ~80o such that the luminal-side 2/3rd (TM10b) of the helix is parallel to TM2 and the cytosolic-side 1/3rd (TM10a) of the helix protrudes between TM2 and TM11 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes a structural feature of TM10.

claim: The bending of TM10 is aided by P575 and G576, residues known to induce helix breaks and kinks.
source: The bending of TM10 is aided by P575 and G576, residues are known to induce helix breaks and kinks (Javadpour et al., 1999; Ulmschneider and Sansom, 2001).
evidence: This explains the structural basis for TM10 bending, supported by citations about proline and glycine effects on helices.

claim: The authors found density in the cryo-EM map overlapping the MOLEonline prediction in both protomers, spanning the entire length of TMD, that allowed unambiguous modeling of a single acetyl-CoA.
source: We find a density in our cryo-EM map overlapping the MOLEonline prediction in both protomers, spanning the entire length of TMD, that allowed us to unambiguously model a single acetyl-CoA, such that the 3', 5'-ADP nucleoside head group is towards the cytosol and the acetyl group is hydrogen bonded (~3.5 Å) to N258 of TM2 that is located at the luminal entrance of ACOS.
evidence: This describes the identification and modeling of acetyl-CoA in the structure.

claim: In the HGSNAT structure, the 3', 5'-ADP nucleoside head group of acetyl-CoA is towards the cytosol and the acetyl group is hydrogen bonded (~3.5 Å) to N258 of TM2.
source: We find a density in our cryo-EM map overlapping the MOLEonline prediction in both protomers, spanning the entire length of TMD, that allowed us to unambiguously model a single acetyl-CoA, such that the 3', 5'-ADP nucleoside head group is towards the cytosol and the acetyl group is hydrogen bonded (~3.5 Å) to N258 of TM2 that is located at the luminal entrance of ACOS.
evidence: This describes the orientation and interactions of acetyl-CoA in the structure.

claim: The catalytic H269 is ~4.5 Å away from the acetyl group of acetyl-CoA.
source: The catalytic H269, which is predicted to be acetylated during the acetyltransferase reaction, is ~4.5 Å away from the acetyl group of acetyl-CoA, nestled within the negative charge on the luminal opening, and is ergonomically positioned to perform acetyltransferase reaction in the presence of the acetyl group acceptor (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes the position of the catalytic residue relative to the substrate.

claim: H269 is predicted to be acetylated during the acetyltransferase reaction.
source: The catalytic H269, which is predicted to be acetylated during the acetyltransferase reaction, is ~4.5 Å away from the acetyl group of acetyl-CoA, nestled within the negative charge on the luminal opening, and is ergonomically positioned to perform acetyltransferase reaction in the presence of the acetyl group acceptor (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on prior biochemical studies cited earlier in the manuscript.

claim: H269 is ergonomically positioned to perform acetyltransferase reaction in the presence of the acetyl group acceptor.
source: The catalytic H269, which is predicted to be acetylated during the acetyltransferase reaction, is ~4.5 Å away from the acetyl group of acetyl-CoA, nestled within the negative charge on the luminal opening, and is ergonomically positioned to perform acetyltransferase reaction in the presence of the acetyl group acceptor (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural positioning of H269.

claim: The binding pocket shows a polarity of charge, changing from positive to neutral to negative as one moves from the cytosolic side to the luminal side.
source: The binding pocket, like the rest of the protein, shows a polarity of charge. As we move from the cytosolic side to the luminal side, the charge changes from positive to neutral to negative (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and D).
evidence: This describes the electrostatic properties of the binding pocket.

claim: The cytosolic opening of the ACOS is comprised of basic and nonpolar amino acids, making it an ideal pocket for binding the 3', 5'-ADP head group.
source: The cytosolic opening of the site is comprised of basic and nonpolar amino acids, making it an ideal pocket for binding the 3', 5'-ADP head group.
evidence: This is an inference about the chemical complementarity between the pocket and the ligand.

claim: The pantothenate group of acetyl-CoA is supported by a network of nonpolar amino acids at the center of the binding pocket.
source: The pantothenate group of acetyl-CoA is supported by a network of nonpolar amino acids at the center of the binding pocket (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and D).
evidence: This describes interactions between acetyl-CoA and the protein.

claim: A series of conserved salt bridges stabilize the cytosolic and luminal entrances of the pore.
source: A series of conserved salt bridges stabilize the cytosolic and luminal entrances of the pore.
evidence: This describes structural features that stabilize the active site.

claim: The luminal entrance is lined with salt bridges between the residues H269, D279, R344, D469, E471, H586, and E587.
source: The luminal entrance is lined with salt bridges between the residues H269, D279, R344, D469, E471, H586, and E587.
evidence: This describes specific salt bridges at the luminal entrance.

claim: The cytosolic entrance is lined with salt bridges between the residues R239, D244, R247, R317, E363, K491, and K634.
source: The cytosolic entrance is lined with salt bridges between the residues R239, D244, R247, R317, E363, K491, and K634 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This describes specific salt bridges at the cytosolic entrance.

claim: A portion of CL1 towards the TM2 and C-terminus of the protein is part of the cytosolic entrance of the ACOS.
source: A portion of CL1 towards the TM2 and C-terminus of the protein also seems to be a part of the cytosolic entrance of the ACOS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural proximity of CL1 to the ACOS.

claim: Sequence conservation between HGSNAT and other known acetyl-CoA binding proteins or transferases is poor.
source: Sequence conservation between HGSNAT and other known acetyl-CoA binding proteins or transferases is poor.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison analyses.

claim: There are no structural homologs of HGSNAT.
source: There are no structural homologs of HGSNAT, and a search within the database of known structures using the HGSNAT TMD by the Dali server resulted in hits with sequence identity of <17% across alignments of <25% sequence length (Holm et al., 2023).
evidence: This is based on structural similarity searches using the Dali server.

claim: A search within the database of known structures using the HGSNAT TMD by the Dali server resulted in hits with sequence identity of <17% across alignments of <25% sequence length.
source: There are no structural homologs of HGSNAT, and a search within the database of known structures using the HGSNAT TMD by the Dali server resulted in hits with sequence identity of <17% across alignments of <25% sequence length (Holm et al., 2023).
evidence: This describes the results of a structural similarity search.

claim: A search with just the luminal domain yields hits with <15% identity over alignments of at least 70% sequence lengths.
source: Even the search with just the luminal domain, which appeared to be a classic two-sheet β-sandwich, yields hits with <15% identity over alignments of at least 70% sequence lengths (Supplementary file 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This describes the results of a structural similarity search for the LD.

claim: The authors used ModelAngelo, a machine-learning-based de novo automatic model-building algorithm, to build the initial HGSNAT model into the cryo-EM density.
source: We used ModelAngelo, a machine-learning-based de novo automatic model-building algorithm to build the initial HGSNAT model into the cryo-EM density (Jamali et al., 2023).
evidence: This describes the computational method used for model building.

claim: The model built by ModelAngelo into the experimental data superposed well with the HGSNAT model as predicted by AlphaFold with a Cα RMSD of ~1.7 Å over 533 amino acids.
source: The model built by ModelAngelo into the experimental data superposed well with the HGSNAT model as predicted by AlphaFold with a Cα RMSD of ~1.7 Å over 533 amino acids (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Jumper et al., 2021; Varadi et al., 2022).
evidence: This compares the experimental structure with the AlphaFold prediction.

claim: HGSNATs of representatives from archaea, bacteria, and plants suggest that LD and TM1 are absent in other kingdoms.
source: HGSNATs of representatives from archaea, bacteria, and plants suggest that LD and TM1 are absent in other kingdoms.
evidence: This is based on sequence and structure comparisons with homologs from other organisms.

claim: HGSNAT homologs from archaea, bacteria, and plants superpose onto the TMD part of HGSNAT, especially TM2-11 with Cα RMSDs of 1–1.4 Å over 350 amino acids.
source: These homologs superpose onto the TMD part of HGSNAT, especially TM2-11 with Cα RMSDs of 1–1.4 Å over 350 amino acids (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes structural conservation across kingdoms.

claim: The TmAT superfamily of membrane proteins consists of two subfamilies: the acyltransferase-3/acetyl-CoA transporter (ATAT) family (TCDB: 9.B.97) and the integral membrane acetyltransferase (YeiB) family (TCDB: 9.B.169).
source: TmAT superfamily of membrane proteins consists of two subfamilies of integral membrane proteins consisting of 8–12 TMs – the acyltransferase-3/acetyl-CoA transporter (ATAT) family (TCDB: 9.B.97) and the integral membrane acetyltransferase (YeiB) family (TCDB: 9.B.169).
evidence: This describes the classification of the TmAT superfamily.

claim: HGSNAT belongs to the YeiB family.
source: HGSNAT belongs to the YeiB family.
evidence: This classifies HGSNAT within the TmAT superfamily.

claim: A meaningful sequence alignment could not be generated between the members of the ATAT and YeiB families.
source: A meaningful sequence alignment could not be generated between the members of these two families.
evidence: This describes the lack of sequence similarity between the two families.

claim: A bent helix near the predicted acetyl-CoA binding site is observed in the ATAT family, suggesting that this could be a conserved feature amongst the members of the TmAT superfamily.
source: Incidentally, a bent helix near the predicted acetyl-CoA binding site is also observed in the ATAT family, suggesting that this could be a conserved feature amongst the members of the TmAT superfamily (Newman et al., 2023).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison with ATAT family members.

claim: The LD and TM1 regions have poor sequence conservation compared to the rest of the protein.
source: It appears that the LD and TM1 regions have poor sequence conservation compared to the rest of the protein (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on sequence conservation analysis shown in a figure.

claim: The authors mapped known clinical mutations (missense, nonsense, and polymorphisms) of HGSNAT onto its three-dimensional structure.
source: We mapped the known clinical mutations (missense, nonsense, and polymorphisms) of HGSNAT onto its three-dimensional structure (Canals et al., 2011; Fan et al., 2006; Fedele and Hopwood, 2010; Feldhammer et al., 2009a; Feldhammer et al., 2009b; Hrebícek et al., 2006; Huizing and Gahl, 2020).
evidence: This describes an analysis combining structural and clinical data.

claim: Almost all the mutations fall within the conserved regions on HGSNAT.
source: Almost all the mutations fall within the conserved regions on HGSNAT (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an observation from mapping mutations onto the conservation analysis.

claim: The nonsense mutations seem to be located more on the cytosolic side, and the missense mutations seem to be populated on the luminal side of HGSNAT.
source: The nonsense mutations seem to be located more on the cytosolic side, and the missense mutations seem to be populated on the luminal side of HGSNAT (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an observation from mapping mutations onto the structure.

claim: The authors estimated the extent of destabilization or stabilization introduced by variants on HGSNAT structure using FoldX.
source: We estimated the extent of destabilization or stabilization introduced by these variants on HGSNAT structure by FoldX, a force field algorithm to evaluate the effect of mutations on the stability and dynamics of proteins (Supplementary file 2; Schymkowitz et al., 2005).
evidence: This describes a computational analysis of mutation effects.

claim: Most destabilizing mutations appear to be concentrated near the LD-TMD interface.
source: We classified these mutations into four groups based on their position on the structure and found that most destabilizing mutations appear to be concentrated near the LD-TMD interface (Figure 4 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the FoldX analysis and structural mapping.

claim: Five missense mutations - E471K (LL3), R344C/R344H (LL2), P283L (TM3), and N258I (TM2) - have been identified in the residues that line the ACOS.
source: Five missense mutations - E471K (LL3), R344C/R344H (LL2), P283L (TM3), and N258I (TM2) - have been identified in the residues that line the ACOS (Figures 4B and 3A, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This lists mutations in the active site region.

claim: E471K mutation could impact the binding affinity of acetyl-CoA because E471 is close to the acetyl group and the mutation changes an acidic to basic side chain.
source: E471 is close to the acetyl group of acetyl-CoA, and acidic to basic side chain substitution in an E471K mutation could impact the binding affinity of acetyl-CoA.
evidence: This is an inference about the effect of the mutation based on the structure.

claim: N258I mutation could directly impact the binding of acetyl-CoA and acetyltransferase activity because N258 is hydrogen bonded to acetyl-CoA.
source: N258 side chain can act as both hydrogen acceptor or donor and is hydrogen bonded to acetyl-CoA in the structure. N258I mutation could directly impact the binding of acetyl-CoA and acetyltransferase activity.
evidence: This is an inference about the effect of the mutation based on the structure.

claim: R344C/R344H mutations could affect the integrity of the luminal entrance of ACOS because R344 forms salt bridges with E469 and E471 that stabilize the luminal entrance.
source: R344 forms salt bridges with E469 and E471 that stabilize the luminal entrance of ACOS. The mutations of R344C/R344H could affect the integrity of the luminal entrance of ACOS.
evidence: This is an inference about the effect of the mutations based on the structure.

claim: P283L mutation could alter the TM3 conformation on the luminal side and thus affect acetyl-CoA binding.
source: P283 is not directly involved in the binding of acetyl-CoA. However, the residues flanking P283 – V281, F282, F285, I288, and M289 – all interact with the pantothenate group of acetyl-CoA (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D). Proline residues define helix conformation, and mutation of a relatively conserved proline to an aliphatic leucine could alter the TM3 conformation on the luminal side and thus affect acetyl-CoA binding.
evidence: This is an inference about the effect of the mutation based on structural considerations.

claim: FoldX prediction indicates that P283L is the most destabilizing of all ACOS mutations.
source: FoldX prediction indicates that P283L is the most destabilizing of all ACOS mutations perhaps because it impacts the TM3 conformation.
evidence: This is a result from the FoldX computational analysis.

claim: N258I and R344H substitutions did not reduce the overall expression of HGSNAT.
source: We generated N258I and R344H mutants to test the effect of these substitutions on the expression and stability of HGSNAT. We noticed that these substitutions did not reduce the overall expression of HGSNAT (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation about mutant expression.

claim: R344H mutant showed slightly enhanced aggregation upon solubilization in 1% digitonin but the overall stability was not drastically altered compared to WT HGSNAT.
source: R344H mutant, upon solubilization in 1% digitonin, showed slightly enhanced aggregation but the overall stability of R344H mutant was not altered drastically, compared to WT HGSNAT (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and I, and 1 L).
evidence: This is an experimental observation about the R344H mutant.

claim: Although the N258I mutant showed expression comparable to WT HGSNAT, no peak for N258I nor free GFP could be observed in FSEC.
source: Although the N258I mutant showed expression comparable to WT HGSNAT, as evident by total fluorescence measurements of solubilized cell lysates, we could not observe any peak for N258I nor free GFP in FSEC (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation about the N258I mutant.

claim: N258I substitution directly affected the substrate binding and stability, resulting in the unstable protein being pelleted out of solution upon solubilization followed by ultracentrifugation.
source: We hypothesize that N258I substitution directly affected the substrate binding and stability. As a result, upon solubilization followed by ultracentrifugation, the unstable protein got pelleted out of the solution (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the experimental observations for N258I.

claim: C76F, G262R, N273K, G423W, and G424S/G424V are all missense mutations that are on the LD-TMD interface.
source: C76F, G262R, N273K, G423W, and G424S/G424V are all missense mutations that are on the LD-TMD interface, and our FoldX-based analysis indicates these mutations to be the most destabilizing among the ones that we listed.
evidence: This identifies mutations at the LD-TMD interface and their predicted effects.

claim: FoldX-based analysis indicates that C76F, G262R, G423W, and G424S/G424V mutations are the most destabilizing among the mutations analyzed.
source: C76F, G262R, N273K, G423W, and G424S/G424V are all missense mutations that are on the LD-TMD interface, and our FoldX-based analysis indicates these mutations to be the most destabilizing among the ones that we listed.
evidence: This is a result from the FoldX computational analysis.

claim: N273K is predicted to be least destabilizing by FoldX among the LD-TMD interface mutations.
source: N273K is predicted to be least destabilizing by FoldX, as all these mutations, except N273K, result in charge reversal and drastic change in the side chain size, leading to steric clashes and breakdown of existing interactions (Figures 4B and 2B).
evidence: This is a result from the FoldX computational analysis with structural explanation.

claim: C76F mutation reduces the expression of the protein, suggesting that LD-TMD interaction is essential for proper folding and stability of HGSNAT.
source: C76F mutation reduces the expression of the protein, suggesting that LD-TMD interaction is essential for proper folding and stability of HGSNAT (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation and inference about the importance of the LD-TMD interface.

claim: W403C, M482K, G486E, A489E, S518F, S539C, and S541L are all mutations that occur in the scaffold domain (TM6-TM9) of HGSNAT.
source: W403C, M482K, G486E, A489E, S518F, S539C, and S541L are all mutations that occur in the scaffold domain (TM6-TM9) of HGSNAT.
evidence: This identifies mutations in the scaffold domain.

claim: FoldX predicts scaffold domain mutations to be only mildly destabilizing.
source: FoldX predicts these mutations to be only mildly destabilizing.
evidence: This is a result from the FoldX computational analysis.

claim: W403C was mildly destabilizing, with reduced thermal stability compared to WT HGSNAT but no effect on overall expression.
source: Corroborating the FoldX prediction, we noticed that W403C was mildly destabilizing. While the overall expression of the W403C mutant was not affected, the thermal stability was reduced compared to WT HGSNAT (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,G,I and M).
evidence: This is an experimental observation confirming the FoldX prediction.

claim: HGSNAT was purified at pH 7.5 without adding acetyl-CoA to the buffer.
source: HGSNAT, in this report, was purified at pH 7.5. During the purification process, we did not add acetyl-CoA to the buffer.
evidence: This describes the purification conditions.

claim: The authors confirmed the presence of endogenously bound acetyl-CoA in the cryo-EM sample by LC-MS.
source: However, we were able to confirm the presence of endogenously bound acetyl-CoA in our cryo-EM sample by LC-MS (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental confirmation of acetyl-CoA binding.

claim: Acetyl-CoA binding happens on the cytosolic side and is optimal around pH 7.0–8.0.
source: It has been demonstrated, previously, that acetyl-CoA binding happens on the cytosolic side and is optimal around pH 7.0–8.0, and the acetyl transfer activity happens on the luminal side and is optimal at pH 5.5–6.0.
evidence: This summarizes prior biochemical findings.

claim: The acetyl transfer activity happens on the luminal side and is optimal at pH 5.5–6.0.
source: It has been demonstrated, previously, that acetyl-CoA binding happens on the cytosolic side and is optimal around pH 7.0–8.0, and the acetyl transfer activity happens on the luminal side and is optimal at pH 5.5–6.0.
evidence: This summarizes prior biochemical findings.

claim: The Km of N-acetyltransferase reaction in the presence of acetyl-CoA as the substrate is in the 0.2–0.6 mM range at pH 5–5.8, and 2.5–20 μM range at pH 7.0.
source: The Km of N-acetyltransferase reaction in the presence of acetyl-CoA as the substrate is in the 0.2–0.6 mM range at pH 5–5.8, and 2.5–20 μM range at pH 7.0, suggesting that HGSNAT has a high affinity for acetyl-CoA at pH >7.0 (Bame and Rome, 1985; Bame and Rome, 1986a; Meikle et al., 1995).
evidence: This cites prior biochemical measurements.

claim: HGSNAT has a high affinity for acetyl-CoA at pH >7.0.
source: The Km of N-acetyltransferase reaction in the presence of acetyl-CoA as the substrate is in the 0.2–0.6 mM range at pH 5–5.8, and 2.5–20 μM range at pH 7.0, suggesting that HGSNAT has a high affinity for acetyl-CoA at pH >7.0 (Bame and Rome, 1985; Bame and Rome, 1986a; Meikle et al., 1995).
evidence: This is an inference from the Km values cited.

claim: The transfer of the acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to the terminal non-reducing amino group of α-D-glucosamine is believed to be catalyzed by H269 located on the luminal entrance of ACOS.
source: The transfer of the acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to the terminal non-reducing amino group of α-D-glucosamine is believed to be catalyzed by H269 located on the luminal entrance of ACOS (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the proposed catalytic mechanism based on prior work.

claim: It is unclear if H269 gets acetylated and forms a stable acetylated intermediate in the process of acetyl transfer.
source: It is unclear if H269 gets acetylated and forms a stable acetylated intermediate in the process of acetyl transfer.
evidence: This describes uncertainty in the field about the reaction mechanism.

claim: For H269 to be acetylated or to transfer the acetyl group to its putative acceptor, protonation of the imidazole sidechain amine group is necessary.
source: However, for the H269 to be acetylated or for it to transfer the acetyl group to its putative acceptor, protonation of the imidazole sidechain amine group is necessary.
evidence: This is based on chemical principles of catalysis.

claim: The catalytic H269 is primarily uncharged at pH 7.5.
source: The catalytic H269 is primarily uncharged at pH 7.5, and the acetyl-CoA remains an acetate ion.
evidence: This is based on the pKa of histidine and the pH of the sample.

claim: In the HGSNAT structure, acetyl-CoA is hydrogen-bonded to N258.
source: In our structure, ACOS is more accessible from the luminal side than the cytosolic entrance. We note that the acetyl-CoA is hydrogen-bonded to N258 (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This describes an observation from the structure.

claim: The structure represents an acetyl-CoA primed HGSNAT waiting for the protonation of H269 and the availability of an acetyl group acceptor to carry out acetyltransferase reaction.
source: Based on these observations, we conclude that the structure we have is of an acetyl-CoA primed HGSNAT waiting for the protonation of H269 and the availability of an acetyl group acceptor to carry out acetyltransferase reaction (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural and biochemical data.

claim: The acetyl-CoA primed conformation is the most stable conformation of HGSNAT in the absence of an acetyl group acceptor because the cytosolic pH is favorable for acetyl-CoA binding and the protein endogenously pulled down acetyl-CoA.
source: Because the cytosolic pH is favorable for acetyl-CoA binding and the protein we purified endogenously pulled down acetyl-CoA with it, we believe this is the most stable conformation of HGSNAT in the absence of an acetyl group acceptor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the purification conditions and endogenous ligand binding.

claim: H269A substitution did not alter the expression nor stability of HGSNAT.
source: Furthermore, in our FSEC-based analysis, we noticed that H269A substitution did neither alter the expression nor stability of HGSNAT (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,D and J).
evidence: This is an experimental observation about the H269A mutant.

claim: N258I mutation completely destabilized HGSNAT.
source: However, the N258I mutation completely destabilized HGSNAT (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation about the N258I mutant.

claim: N258 has a greater role in acetyl-CoA binding than H269 based on the structure.
source: We believe N258I instability to be a consequence of lack of substrate binding at the catalytic core, as we see a greater role for N258 in acetyl-CoA binding as opposed to H269 as per our structure (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural interactions and mutant phenotypes.

claim: Direct involvement of acetyl-CoA in heparan sulfate degradation was shown in the early 1980s by incubating extracted intact lysosomes with radiolabeled acetyl-CoA and monitoring the incorporation of radiolabeled acetate into lysosomal HS.
source: Direct involvement of acetyl-CoA in the heparan sulfate degradation was shown in the early 1980 s, by incubating the extracted intact lysosomes with radiolabeled acetyl-CoA and by subsequently monitoring the incorporation of radiolabeled acetate into lysosomal HS (Rome and Crain, 1981; Rome et al., 1983).
evidence: This summarizes historical biochemical experiments, supported by citations.

claim: Rome and colleagues showed that the acetyl-CoA-dependent N-acetyltransferase activity resides on the lysosomal membrane using purified lysosomal membranes.
source: Using purified lysosomal membranes, Rome and colleagues showed that the acetyl-CoA-dependent N-acetyltransferase activity, which is required for acetylation of HS, resides on the lysosomal membrane.
evidence: This summarizes prior biochemical findings, supported by citations.

claim: Rome and colleagues suggested that the HS acetylation reaction occurs in two steps - acetylation of the lysosomal membranes and transfer of acetyl from the membranes to HS.
source: In these studies, they also suggested that the HS acetylation reaction occurs in two steps - acetylation of the lysosomal membranes and transfer of acetyl from the membranes to HS.
evidence: This summarizes a mechanistic proposal from prior work.

claim: Rome and colleagues showed that the acetylation process is optimal at pH 7, acetyltransferase activity is optimal at pH 5.5, and the amino acid on the lysosomal membrane that gets acetylated is a histidine.
source: By performing acetylation and acetyltransferase reactions at different pH, and in the presence of different amino acid modification reagents, they showed that the acetylation process is optimal at pH 7, acetyltransferase activity is optimal at pH 5.5, and the amino acid on the lysosomal membrane that gets acetylated is a histidine.
evidence: This summarizes biochemical findings from prior work.

claim: Rome and colleagues proposed that the N-acetyltransferase activity follows a Ping Pong Bi Bi mechanism of reaction.
source: They proposed that the N-acetyltransferase activity follows a Ping Pong Bi Bi mechanism of reaction, where acetyl-CoA from the cytosol acetylates the active site histidine of the N-acetyltransferase located on the lysosomal membrane, inducing a conformational change in the transmembrane enzyme that enables the access of active site histidine from the luminal side (Figure 5D).
evidence: This summarizes a mechanistic proposal from prior work.

claim: Pshezhetsky and colleagues showed that acetylation of lysosomal membranes expressing N-acetyltransferase activity occurred even in the absence of the acetyl group acceptor, suggesting the formation of an acetylated enzyme intermediate.
source: Pshezhetsky and colleagues showed that acetylation of lysosomal membranes expressing N-acetyltransferase activity occurred even in the absence of the acetyl group acceptor, suggesting the formation of an acetylated enzyme intermediate (Ausseil et al., 2006; Durand et al., 2010).
evidence: This summarizes biochemical findings from prior work, supported by citations.

claim: In the HGSNAT structure, H269 of LL1 is not acetylated.
source: In our structure, we find that the HGSNAT ACOS is more accessible via the lumen as opposed to the cytosol and that the His269 of LL1 is not acetylated.
evidence: This is an observation from the structure.

claim: The authors believe N258 holds onto acetyl-CoA and aids H269 in the acetyltransferase reaction at low pH and in the availability of acetyl group acceptor.
source: We believe N258 holds onto acetyl-CoA and aids H269 in the acetyltransferase reaction, at low pH and in the availability of acetyl group acceptor.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the roles of N258 and H269 based on the structure.

claim: Meikle and colleagues argued that the N-acetyltransferase reaction occurs via a random-order mechanism.
source: Meikle and colleagues argued that the N-acetyltransferase reaction occurs via a random-order mechanism (Figure 5C).
evidence: This summarizes a mechanistic proposal from prior work.

claim: Meikle and colleagues demonstrated that both N-acetyl-α-D-glucosamine and COA are required for the reverse reaction, suggesting that the formation of a ternary complex enables the reaction to proceed in a single step without the requirement of an acetylated-enzyme intermediate.
source: They demonstrated that both N-acetyl-α-D-glucosamine and COA are required for the reverse reaction, suggesting that the formation of a ternary complex of acetyl-CoA, α-D-glucosamine, and the enzyme enables the reaction to proceed in a single step without the requirement of an acetylated-enzyme intermediate.
evidence: This summarizes biochemical findings from prior work.

claim: Meikle and colleagues reported two Km values that differ by 5–10 times for both acetyl-CoA and glucosamine substrates, suggesting that both protomers bind to the substrates at varying affinity and only one of the protomers is catalyzing the acetyl transfer at any given point of time.
source: They also report two Km values, that differ by 5–10 times, for both acetyl-CoA and glucosamine substrates, suggesting that both protomers, perhaps, bind to the substrates at varying affinity and only one of the protomers is catalyzing the acetyl transfer at any given point of time (Meikle et al., 1995).
evidence: This summarizes biochemical findings and their interpretation from prior work.

claim: Mahuran and colleagues showed that acetylated enzyme intermediate could not be identified by affinity pulldown of purified transmembrane N-acetyltransferase after incubating it with [3H] acetyl-CoA.
source: Mahuran and colleagues showed that acetylated enzyme intermediate could not be identified by affinity pulldown of purified transmembrane N-acetyltransferase after incubating it with [3H] acetyl-CoA and proposed that the formation of a stable acetylated enzyme intermediate is not required for the reaction to proceed (Fan et al., 2011).
evidence: This summarizes biochemical findings from prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: The HGSNAT structure does not provide evidence of H269 acetylation.
source: Our structure does not provide evidence of H269 acetylation (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure.

claim: Acetyl-CoA binds tightly to HGSNAT endogenously, resulting in a stable HGSNAT-acetyl-CoA intermediate that stayed intact through purification.
source: However, we observe that acetyl-CoA binds tightly to HGSNAT endogenously resulting in a stable HGSNAT-acetyl-CoA intermediate that stayed as an intact complex all through the affinity purification, size-exclusion chromatography, and cryo-EM sample preparation steps even without the addition of exogenous acetyl-CoA to any of the buffers (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the purification and LC-MS analysis.

claim: The tight endogenous binding of acetyl-CoA to HGSNAT is the reason why Mahuran and colleagues could not observe the labeling of purified transmembrane N-acetyltransferase by [3H] acetyl-CoA.
source: Perhaps, this tight endogenous binding of HGSNAT is the reason why Mahuran and colleagues could not observe the labeling of purified transmembrane N-acetyltransferase by [3H] acetyl-CoA.
evidence: This is a speculation to reconcile the current findings with prior work.

claim: The structure obtained does not by itself settle the debate about the mechanism of HGSNAT-mediated acetylation.
source: The structure that we obtained does not by itself settle the debate about the mechanism of HGSNAT-mediated acetylation.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the current structure in resolving mechanistic questions.

claim: The HGSNAT structure is in a conformation that could proceed through any of the three enzyme-catalyzed bisubstrate reaction mechanisms for acetyl transfer.
source: Our structure is in a conformation that could proceed through any of the three enzyme-catalyzed bisubtrate reaction mechanisms for acetyl transfer (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data in the context of possible mechanisms.

claim: While the manuscript was being revised, another group published structures of apo HGSNAT and HGSNAT-ACO, HGSNAT-COA-NAG complexes.
source: While we were revising our manuscript, another group published structures of apo HGSNAT and HGSNAT-ACO, HGSNAT-COA-NAG complexes.
evidence: This acknowledges concurrent work by another group.

claim: The structures published by Xu and colleagues were obtained at pH 8.0 in 1% GDN and revealed no drastic conformational isomerization in the protein except for localized motion in TM2 and TM3 and residues at ACOS.
source: All these structures were obtained at pH 8.0 in 1% GDN and revealed no drastic conformational isomerization in the protein except for localized motion in TM2 and TM3 and residues at ACOS (Xu et al., 2024).
evidence: This summarizes findings from the concurrent work, supported by a citation.

claim: Xu and colleagues do not show if the order of binding of the substrate is crucial for catalysis, and nor do they disprove the existence of acetylated enzyme intermediate.
source: Xu and colleagues do not show if the order of binding of the substrate is crucial for catalysis, and nor do they disprove the existence of acetylated enzyme intermediate.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the concurrent work.

claim: Structures of HGSNAT at lysosomal luminal pH in the presence and absence of an acetyl group acceptor will demonstrate if the enzyme gets acetylated during the reaction and if there are pH-driven conformational changes within the protein.
source: We believe structures of HGSNAT at lysosomal luminal pH in the presence and absence of an acetyl group acceptor will demonstrate not only if the enzyme gets acetylated during the reaction but also show if there are pH-driven conformational changes within the protein.
evidence: This is a speculation about future experiments needed to resolve mechanistic questions.

claim: It is likely that the choice of detergent used determines the conformational isomerization of HGSNAT.
source: It is also likely that the choice of detergent used determines the conformational isomerization.
evidence: This is a speculation about factors affecting protein conformation.

claim: Obtaining structures in membrane mimetics like nanodiscs in the presence of native HGSNAT lipids could provide a clearer insight into HGSNAT catalyzed reaction mechanism.
source: So, obtaining structures in membrane mimetics like nanodiscs in the presence of native HGSNAT lipids could provide a clearer insight into HGSNAT catalyzed reaction mechanism.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future experiments.

claim: According to the structure, C123 and C434 are ~34 Å apart, making a disulfide bond between them impossible in the acetyl-CoA bound HGSNAT conformation.
source: However, according to the structure, these amino acids are ~34 Å apart making such a bond impossibility in the acetyl-CoA bound HGSNAT conformation reported here (Figures 1A, D, 2B).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure that contradicts a prior proposal.

claim: C434 is disulfide bonded to C415 on LL3 in the HGSNAT structure.
source: Moreover, we notice that C434 is disulfide bonded to C415 on LL3.
evidence: This is an observation from the structure.

claim: C123 of β6 is predicted to form a disulfide bond with C151 of β8, but density to model such a disulfide was not observed.
source: C123 of β6 is predicted to form a disulfide bond with C151 of β8, and we do not see density to model such a disulfide.
evidence: This describes a predicted disulfide that could not be confirmed in the structure.

claim: A bond between C123 of LD and C434 of LL3 could be a possibility only if there is a drastic conformational change that brings LD closer to LL3.
source: A bond between C123 of LD and C434 of LL3 could be a possibility only if there is a drastic conformational change during that brings LD closer to the LL3.
evidence: This is a speculation about conditions under which the proposed disulfide could form.

claim: The authors believe that α-HGSNAT and β-HGSNAT stay together because of a series of hydrogen bonds, dipole-dipole and hydrophobic interactions between β2-β3 turn, β4-β5 turn, LL1, LL3, and LL4.
source: Thus, we believe that the α-HGSNAT and β-HGSNAT stay together because of a series of hydrogen bonds, dipole-dipole and hydrophobic interactions between β2-β3 turn, β4-β5 turn, LL1, LL3, and LL4 (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed interactions in the structure.

claim: The protease that cleaves HGSNAT into α-HGSNAT and β-HGSNAT is unknown, and the site for proteolysis is unclear.
source: The protease that cleaves HGSNAT into α-HGSNAT and β-HGSNAT is unknown, and the site for proteolysis is unclear.
evidence: This describes gaps in current knowledge.

claim: Fan et al. proposed that the site of proteolysis is between amino acids N144 and G145 in the LD.
source: Fan et al, proposed that the site of proteolysis is between amino acids N144 and G145 in the LD (Fan et al., 2011).
evidence: This summarizes a proposal from prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: Durand et al. proposed that the site of proteolysis is between the end of the luminal domain and the beginning of LL1.
source: Durand et al, proposed that the site of proteolysis is between the end of the luminal domain and the beginning of LL1 (Durand et al., 2010).
evidence: This summarizes a proposal from prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: Sequence-based protease site prediction in Procleave and Prosper servers suggests multiple potential sites of proteolysis between β8 of LD and LL1.
source: Sequence-based protease site prediction in Procleave and Prosper servers, using the sequence between β8 of LD and LL1, suggests multiple potential sites of proteolysis, for example, L154-A155 at the C-term of β8, S162-N163 in the loop connecting LD to TM1, F170-L171 at the N-term of TM1, L187-S188, and W231-R232 at the N- and C-term of the CL1 (Li et al., 2020; Song et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes results from computational predictions.

claim: The recombinant HGSNAT produced is a non-proteolyzed form of HGSNAT.
source: The recombinant HGSNAT that we produced is a non-proteolyzed form of HGSNAT, as we see a band corresponding to full-length HGSNAT in our SDS-PAGE analysis and a peak corresponding to an intact full-length dimer in our FSEC analysis.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data.

claim: HGSNAT is encoded by 18 exons, where the first 6 exons encode an N-terminal LD & TM1, which are only present in the metazoans.
source: HGSNAT is encoded by 18 exons, where the first 6 exons encode an N-terminal LD & TM1, which are only present in the metazoans.
evidence: This describes the genomic organization and evolutionary conservation of HGSNAT.

claim: The remaining 10 TMs and the C-terminus of HGSNAT are well conserved in archaea, bacteria, and plants.
source: The remaining 10 TMs and the C-terminus are well conserved in archaea, bacteria, and plants (Fan et al., 2006; Hrebícek et al., 2006).
evidence: This describes evolutionary conservation, supported by citations.

claim: Based on evolutionary sequence and structure conservation and conformational flexibility observed in CL1, the authors speculate that LD & TM1 together form α-HGSNAT and TMs 2–11 form β-HGSNAT.
source: Based on the evolutionary sequence and structure conservation and conformational flexibility observed in CL1, we speculate that LD & TM1 together form α-HGSNAT and TMs 2–11 form β-HGSNAT (Figures 2A and 4A, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a speculation based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: There are no known homologs of the LD, and even the strand arrangement in two sheets appears to be rare.
source: There are no known homologs of the LD, and even the strand arrangement in two sheets appears to be rare (Koch et al., 1992).
evidence: This describes the novelty of the LD fold, with a citation.

claim: The LD is a new fold of β-sandwich that could be best described as a 'transthyretin-like' fold.
source: Because of these non-trivial dissimilarities of LD with three major types of β-sandwiches, we believe that LD is a new fold of β-sandwich that could be best described as a 'transthyretin-like' fold.
evidence: This is a classification decision based on structural comparisons.

claim: The function of LD remains unknown.
source: The function of LD remains unknown.
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in understanding.

claim: DeepSite predicts the presence of two ligand binding sites in HGSNAT, one that overlaps with the ACOS and the other in the cavity between the two sheets of LD.
source: DeepSite predicts the presence of two ligand binding sites in HGSNAT, one that overlaps with the ACOS and the other in the cavity between the two sheets of LD (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; Jiménez et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes a computational prediction.

claim: It is unclear if LD binds to a ligand and/or a metal ion.
source: However, it is unclear if LD binds to a ligand and/or a metal ion.
evidence: This acknowledges uncertainty about LD function.

claim: The N-acetyltransferase activity of HGSNAT is enhanced in the presence of anionic phospholipids.
source: It has been shown that the N-acetyltransferase activity of HGSNAT is enhanced in the presence of anionic phospholipids (Fan et al., 2011).
evidence: This summarizes a prior finding, supported by a citation.

claim: Unexplained density in the structure could be best explained as ordered lipids or digitonin.
source: We see unexplained density in these regions that could be best explained as ordered lipids or digitonin (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an interpretation of unmodeled density in the structure.

claim: A computational modeling and molecular dynamics simulation study on OafB showed that the periplasmic SGNH domain undergoes large conformational changes and aids in O-antigen acetylation.
source: A recent report of a computational modeling and molecular dynamics simulation study conducted on a model of OafB, a bacterial O-antigen modifying transmembrane acetyltransferase of the ATAT family within the TmAT superfamily, showed that the periplasmic SGNH domain undergoes large conformational changes and aid in O-antigen acetylation (Newman et al., 2023).
evidence: This summarizes findings from a recent study, supported by a citation.

claim: It is possible that the TMDs and the extra-membranous domains of ATAT and YeiB families function similarly despite structural differences.
source: There are non-trivial differences between the predicted structures of ATAT and YeiB family members. However, it is possible that the TMDs and the extra-membranous domains function similarly.
evidence: This is a speculation about functional similarity despite structural differences.

claim: It is likely that LD of HGSNAT binds to HS, stabilizing the terminal non-reducing sugar of HS near the luminal side of ACOS for catalysis.
source: It is likely that LD of HGSNAT binds to HS, stabilizing the terminal non-reducing sugar of HS near the luminal side of ACOS for catalysis and remains to be structurally investigated.
evidence: This is a speculation about LD function based on its position and the enzyme's substrate.

claim: As the size of the acetyl group acceptor was increased from mono- to di- to tetra-saccharide, the Km values decreased from 0.6 mM to 7 μM.
source: In fact, it has been shown that as the size of the acetyl group acceptor was increased in an acetyltransferase reaction from mono- to di- to tetra-saccharide, the Km values decreased from 0.6 mM to 7 μM (Meikle et al., 1995).
evidence: This cites prior biochemical measurements showing substrate size effects.

claim: The high-resolution structure of HGSNAT heralds a new beginning for structural exploration of the TmAT superfamily.
source: The high-resolution structure of HGSNAT reported in this study heralds a new beginning for structural exploration of the TmAT superfamily.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the work.

claim: The conformation of HGSNAT observed in the cryo-EM studies does not put to rest the debate on the kind of bi-substrate reaction mechanism that HGSNAT follows.
source: The conformation of HGSNAT observed in our cryo-EM studies does not put to rest the debate on the kind of bi-substrate reaction mechanism that HGSNAT follows to catalyze the acetyl transfer.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the current work.

claim: The structure underscores the requirement to characterize the remaining states of the enzymatic reaction.
source: However, our structure underscores the requirement to characterize the remaining states of the enzymatic reaction.
evidence: This is a statement about future work needed.

claim: The molecular basis delineated for mutation-induced dysfunction in HGSNAT will serve as a blueprint for the structure-based design of novel therapeutic modulators.
source: The molecular basis we delineated for the mutation-induced dysfunction in HGSNAT will serve as a blueprint for the structure-based design of novel therapeutic modulators that could rescue the function of milder variants.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential applications of the work.
